stem: For a given condition in a population, which of the following correctly distinguishes prevalence from incidence?

options.label: A
options.text: Prevalence: persons who develop it; incidence: persons who have it
options.misconception: Reverses the definitions of prevalence and incidence.
options.explanation: This reverses the two measures: incidence counts persons who develop a condition, and prevalence counts persons who have it.

options.label: B
options.text: Prevalence: persons who develop it; incidence: persons who die of it
options.misconception: Assigns new cases to prevalence and deaths to incidence.
options.explanation: Prevalence counts persons who have a condition, not those who develop it, and deaths are counted by mortality measures, not incidence.

options.label: C
options.text: Prevalence: persons who die of it; incidence: persons who have it
options.misconception: Assigns deaths to prevalence and existing cases to incidence.
options.explanation: Deaths are counted by mortality measures, not prevalence, and persons who have a condition are counted by prevalence, not incidence.

options.label: D
options.text: Prevalence: persons who have it; incidence: persons who develop it
options.misconception: None — prevalence counts who has the condition; incidence counts who develops it.
options.explanation: CDC: prevalence is the proportion of persons who have a condition at or during a period; incidence is the proportion or rate who develop it.

options.label: E
options.text: Prevalence: persons who recover from it; incidence: persons who die of it
options.misconception: Treats prevalence as recovery and incidence as death, confusing both with outcome measures.
options.explanation: Prevalence counts persons who currently have a condition, not those who recovered, and incidence counts new cases, not deaths.

context: Learning objective: Prevalence is the proportion of persons who have a condition; incidence is the proportion or rate who develop it.
